title: The Birth of Jesus
speaker: Josh Wyatt
card_summary: On Christmas Eve, Josh reads Luke 2 as history: God’s Light enters human darkness at the appointed time and place. The manger foreshadows the cross and empty tomb, angels announce peace through the Savior, and shepherds hear, believe, move, and tell. Behold Christ, ponder his work, and trust him with the future.
section_intro: The sermon begins at 00:45 after opening music. Josh follows Luke 2 from the angelic announcement through Bethlehem, the shepherds, heaven’s song, Mary’s pondering, and resurrection foreshadowing, then closes in prayer at 36:48.

movements.heading: Christmas is God’s light entering darkness
bullets: Josh opens with the angelic birth announcement and heaven’s praise. Isaiah’s darkness is not decorative; it names sin, sorrow, pride, and rebellion. God sends himself, and darkness cannot overcome the Light.
Christmas is a historical rescue plan for sin, evil, suffering, sadness, and death. If Christ had first come to destroy all evil, sinful humanity would have been destroyed with it.
He comes first to be rejected, carry the cross, and bear judgment. Redemption precedes his return as the conquering King who destroys evil without destroying the redeemed.

movements.heading: Children, gifts, and Christmas stories
bullets: Josh invites children to name favorite Christmas movies and gives them gifts. Elf and The Grinch establish a contrast between beloved invented stories and Luke’s history.
Unlike tales that begin “once upon a time” or in a distant galaxy, Luke names rulers, places, and public events.

movements.heading: Luke records history planned for Christ
bullets: Caesar Augustus, Quirinius, Syria, registration, and real towns anchor the birth in public history. Josh appeals to ancient historians and asks hearers to treat Scripture as historical testimony.
The day was planned before creation. All things were made through and for Christ, and at the set time God sent the Son for redemption and adoption.
People admire crafted stories, but God writes through time and place. Bethlehem is not Narnia or Naboo; it is a real city where the appointed event occurred.

movements.heading: Providence and prophecy converge in Bethlehem
bullets: Caesar’s census moves Joseph and Mary from Nazareth to David’s city. Caesar issues the decree, but God governs it to fulfill Micah.
Prophecy is like a gift’s shadow: not the gift itself, but a true shape pointing toward what comes. Mary’s surrender joins promises of a human, Jewish, Davidic, virgin-born Savior in Bethlehem.
God weaves promises into history in a way that becomes difficult to ignore. The bread of life is born in Bethlehem, the “house of bread.”

movements.heading: The birth signs reveal the Savior’s purpose
bullets: Luke’s firstborn son, swaddling cloths, and manger carry weight. Josh rejects Mary’s perpetual virginity and urges listeners to test every teaching against Scripture.
No room anticipates Jesus’ rejection. Narrow cloth strips and a stone manger make the living infant resemble a burial scene—arrival foreshadowing the death and resurrection he came to accomplish.
The Lamb of God arrives. Joseph is told to name him Jesus because he saves from sin; the Son of Man’s authority to forgive confirms that God has come in flesh.

movements.heading: Angels announce good news to shepherds
bullets: An angel reveals the sign to shepherds. Josh imagines heaven seeing the author of life cry and the eternal Word as a speechless infant; the rich Christ has become poor for others.
Outcast shepherds tending sacrificial lambs are summoned to God’s once-for-all Lamb. Josh pictures the cave as a temporary holy place where they meet the sacrifice who ends the system.
The angelic sermon is worldwide good news. “Christ” identifies the promised King, Prophet, and Priest; Jesus came to save people, not teach them to save themselves.
He is Savior, Christ, and Lord—the fulfillment of God’s promises, the one who includes Gentiles and reigns from heaven.

movements.heading: The first Christmas carol announces peace with God
bullets: Isaiah’s promised child is born, and the heavenly choir models the fitting response: glory to God and peace among those with whom he is pleased.
Josh explicitly contrasts Luke’s wording with the old King James “peace and goodwill toward men.” Blessings flow broadly, but saving peace belongs to those who receive and trust Christ.
People may experience secondhand benefits through changed believers without resting in peace with God. Salvation is Christ’s gift, not a reward for human goodwill or successful self-rescue.

movements.heading: The shepherds hear, believe, move, and tell
bullets: After the angels depart, the shepherds hurry to Bethlehem, find the sign, report the message, and return praising God while Mary treasures what happened.
Faith acts on revelation: they hear, believe, and move. Those who seek the promised sign find it; those redeemed by Christ naturally go tell what they have seen and heard.
The first evangelists eventually return to ordinary responsibilities, but they return forever changed.

movements.heading: Mary ponders birth and resurrection
bullets: For people carrying loss and struggling to find joy, Josh recommends Mary’s quiet practice: treasure God’s work and ponder it rather than demanding spectacle every day.
Birth and resurrection mirror each other: Mary and Joseph, virgin womb and unused tomb, cloth bands and stone, sorrow turned to joy, spices, angels, and people running to see the sign.
The empty tomb completes the manger’s promise: the living one is not among the dead; he is risen.

Remember first receiving everlasting life. The God who writes through history and empties tombs can be trusted with the future. Perfect love drives out fear; behold Christ repeatedly and walk in Christmas joy daily.

movements.heading: Prayer for lives filled with light
bullets: Josh offers love, obedience, and willingness to be changed. He asks that the church be filled with divine light as it ponders God’s saving work.
He prays that lives will shine brightly in a universe turned from darkness toward light and closes with thanks for Jesus.

ledger.phrase: “For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior who is Christ the Lord … Glory to God in the highest and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased.”
“The people walking in darkness have seen a great light”; Josh applies the darkness to sin, sorrow, pride, and rebellion.
“The light has come and the darkness cannot overcome him.”
At Christ’s return he comes “with a sword” and “on a horse” to destroy sin, death, and evil.
“It’s all a divine setup to destroy the works of Satan.”
“In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus … This was the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria … each to his own town.”
“For in him all things were created … all things have been created through him and for him.”
“When the set time had fully come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem … that we might receive adoption to sonship.”
Joseph goes from Nazareth to Bethlehem, David’s city, to register with Mary, “his betrothed, who was with child.”
God moves Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem “in order to fulfill his word through the prophet Micah.”
“May it be to me according to your word”; Josh calls this Mary’s surrender to God’s will.
The promised Savior would come from Judah and David’s family, be born of a virgin in Bethlehem, and be announced by a star.
“I am the bread of life”; the bread of life is born in Bethlehem, the “house of bread.”

Mary gives birth to her “firstborn son,” wraps him in swaddling cloths, and lays him in a manger “because there was no place for them in the inn”; Josh develops the firstborn, rejection, cloth, and stone-manger details.
“The Lamb of God has arrived”; the burial-like manger scene points to his purpose of conquering death.
“For unto you this day, a Savior is born.”
“She will give birth to a son … name him Jesus because he will save his people from their sins.”
“The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.”
Shepherds keep watch at night; the angel announces “good news of great joy,” the Savior’s birth, and the sign of the wrapped baby in a manger.
Josh describes “the Word of God, the Logos, as a speechless baby.”
“Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor so that you through his poverty might become rich.”
“We have been made holy through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.”
“Fear not … good news of great joy … for all the people … a Savior who is Christ”; Josh stresses the worldwide gospel and explains Christ/Messiah.
“No matter how many promises God has made, they are ‘Yes’ in Christ … the ‘Amen’ is spoken by us to the glory of God.”
Christ would “graft in a most unnatural branch,” referring to Gentile inclusion.
“God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.”
“For to us a child is born … Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.”
“A multitude of the heavenly hosts praising God … ‘Glory to God in the highest and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased.’”
“And on earth peace and goodwill toward men”; Josh explicitly identifies this as the old King James wording and argues that it is inaccurate.
Those who receive peace with God “become a peacemaker” and make peace with others.
Salvation peace is “a gift to those who trust in Jesus, not a reward” for works; people cannot save themselves.
The shepherds go to Bethlehem in haste, find Mary, Joseph, and the baby, spread the message, and return glorifying God; Mary treasures and ponders.
“I love those who love me, and those who seek me find me”; Josh connects this with the shepherds finding the promised sign.
“But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.”
Josh retells the virgin conception and birth: Mary and Joseph, sorrow turned to joy, swaddling bands, stone manger, angels, shepherds, and wise men bringing gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
Joseph of Arimathea wraps Jesus and lays him in an unused stone tomb while Mary Magdalene watches in sorrow.
The women bring spices, angels announce resurrection, and ask, “Why do you look for the living among the dead?”
Hearing Mary’s news, Peter and John run to the tomb and see Jesus’ burial cloths lying in the empty tomb.
“He is not here. He is risen.”
Josh prays that homes will be amazed that “you have peace with God through Jesus Christ.”
“Respond to the angel’s invitation. Fear not.”
“There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear.”
“Fear not. Behold the one God sent to save us from our sin.”
